ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Approval was obtained from the Child and Adolescent Health Service Human Research Ethics Committee (RGS0000000019).
A total of 972 infants were enrolled, 486 in each study arm.
We enrolled healthy infants born on or after 32 weeks gestation.

They were randomised 1:1 to receive either a standard three-dose homologous pertussis priming schedule with a 6-in-1 aP combination vaccine at approximately 6 weeks, 4 months and 6 months old ('aP-only schedule') or a heterologous pertussis priming schedule consisting of a first dose of a WHO-prequalified 5-in-1 wP combination vaccine at 6 weeks old followed by the 6-in-1 aP combination vaccine at 4 months and 6 months old ('mixed wP/aP schedule').

The study protocol and statistical analysis plan have been published previously and are available through open access. [26, 27] Briefly, participants were enrolled between 6 and < 12 weeks old and were randomised with equal probability to the aP-only schedule versus the mixed wP/aP schedule.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: In this multicentre, randomised, participant and outcome assessor-blinded, parallel, two-stage, Bayesian adaptive trial we assigned Australian infants to one of two pertussis vaccination schedules. These consisted of either a standard homologous priming with a hexavalent combination aP vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, aP, hepatitis B, inactivated poliovirus types 1, 2, and 3, and Haemophilus influenzae type b; DTaP-HepB-IPV-Hib) at approximately 6 weeks, 4 months and 6 months old ('aP-only' schedule), or a first dose of a WHO-prequalified pentavalent wP combination vaccine (DTwP-HepB-Hib; Pentabio®, PT Bio Farma Indonesia) at approximately 6 weeks old, followed by hexavalent aP combination vaccine at approximately 4 months and 6 months old ('mixed wP/aP' schedule). The primary outcome was physician-confirmed food allergy by age 12 months requiring both evidence of sensitisation and compatible symptoms in response to either incidental or medically supervised oral food challenge. The initial target sample size was 3,000 enrolments to provide approximately 85% power to detect a policy-relevant 3 percentage point reduction in the risk of the primary outcome.

Under the specified thresholds and assuming 10% incidence of IgE-mediated food allergy by age 12 months in the aP-only group, simulations indicated that enrolling 3,000 infants would ensure 85% power for detecting a 3-percentage point reduction (to 7%) in the mixed wP/aP group. Before any efficacy analyses were conducted, the maximum sample size was revised to 2,000 participants due to slow enrolment and resource constraints. Statistical power was reassessed based on the same thresholds indicating the revised maximum sample size afforded 73% power to detect a 3-percentage point reduction in food allergy (from 10% to 7%). Analyses of the clinical and mechanistic secondary outcomes followed the same approach as the primary outcome. Evidence from mechanistic and observational studies suggests that replacing the first acellular pertussis (aP) vaccine dose in early infancy with a whole-cell pertussis (wP)-containing vaccine may reduce the risk of developing IgE-mediated food allergy during childhood.
We aimed to determine if a dose of wP at approximately 6 weeks old, in lieu of aP vaccine, could reduce the incidence of food allergy in infants.
In this multicentre, randomised, participant and outcome assessor-blinded, parallel, two-stage, Bayesian adaptive trial we assigned Australian infants to one of two pertussis vaccination schedules.

These consisted of either a standard homologous priming with a hexavalent combination aP vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, aP, hepatitis B, inactivated poliovirus types 1, 2, and 3, and Haemophilus influenzae type b; DTaP-HepB-IPV-Hib) at approximately 6 weeks, 4 months and 6 months old ('aP-only' schedule), or a first dose of a WHO-prequalified pentavalent wP combination vaccine (DTwP-HepB-Hib; Pentabio®, PT Bio Farma Indonesia) at approximately 6 weeks old, followed by hexavalent aP combination vaccine at approximately 4 months and 6 months old ('mixed wP/aP' schedule).

The primary outcome was physician-confirmed food allergy by age 12 months requiring both evidence of sensitisation and compatible symptoms in response to either incidental or medically supervised oral food challenge.
The initial target sample size was 3,000 enrolments to provide approximately 85% power to detect a policy-relevant 3 percentage point reduction in the risk of the primary outcome.
A total of 972 infants were enrolled, 486 in each study arm.
Of these, 26 of 486 (5.3%) assigned to the aP-only group and 31 of 486 (6.4%) assigned to the mixed wP/aP schedule met the primary endpoint definition.

The posterior median difference (95% credible interval) in food allergy among recipients of the mixed wP/aP schedule compared to recipients of the aP-only schedule was 0.01 (-0.02, 0.04; probability [<0] 0.25).

IgE-mediated food allergy affects approximately 10% of Australian infants and is a leading cause of anaphylaxis presentations in children, which have increased substantially in the last 25 years. [1, 2] Since 2016, national guidelines have promoted the introduction of solid foods between the ages of 4 and 6 months old. [3] However, compared to the effect of delayed introduction of solids found in clinical trials, the population-level impact of these guidelines on rates of food allergy has been more modest. [4] [5] [6] Food allergies are thought to arise in young children whose immune systems fail to mature into a balanced Th 1 /Th 17 /Th 2 phenotype, with persistence of a Th 2 -skewed phenotype characterised by production of IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13.

Some exposures in early life, like vaccination, might modulate the maturation of immune responses and have emerged as new potential targets for preventing food allergy.
The whole-cell pertussis (wP) vaccine has been a foundational component of the global
Expanded Program of Immunisation since its inception in 1974, and has been administered to at least 1.4 billion children in Gavi-supported countries since 2000.[ 9-11].

However, adverse events following immunisation and heterogeneity in wP vaccine manufacturing processes have dominated considerations in pertussis vaccine policy in recent decades.[ 10,12,13] Despite its high effectiveness in preventing pertussis notifications, Australia progressively withdrew a locally manufactured wP-based combination vaccine from its National Immunisation Program (NIP) between 1997 and 1999 due to reactogenicity concerns, and replaced it with an aP-based combination vaccine.[ 14,15] A three-dose aP-only primary schedule has been used in Australia since the late 1990s, and this schedule is now recommended in most high income countries.

In these settings, aP booster doses and/or maternal pertussis immunisation have been implemented to mitigate waning immunity and protect infants who are too young to be vaccinated.[ 16,17] Conversely, vaccination with wP-based formulations is the primary strategy for preventing severe pertussis disease in infancy in most low-and middle-income countries.[10] wP vaccines induce a Th 1 and Th 17 -polarised immunophenotype which persists into early adulthood,[18] an effect that might be driven by the adjuvant properties of lipopolysaccharide within the whole-killed Bordetella pertussis cells.[ 19] Compared to aP vaccines, wP vaccines have been reported to attenuate IgE-mediated immune responses to diphtheria (DT) and pertussis toxoids (PT) vaccine antigens,[20-22] although data on the effects of wP vaccines on tetanus toxoid (TT) have been conflicting.[ 23,24] We examined Australian children born during the transition from wP to aP vaccines in a case-control study; those who developed IgE-mediated food allergy were less likely to have received wP than aP as their first pertussis vaccine dose in early infancy (odds ratio [OR] 0.77; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.62-0.95).[ 25] Given the apparent in vitro effects of wP versus aP priming on immunophenotype and the association with food allergy we observed in our case-control study, we hypothesised that compared to a standard aP-only vaccine schedule, substituting the first aP vaccine dose with wP would help induce a balanced Th 1 /Th 17 /Th 2 immune profile and thereby prevent the development of food allergy in infants.[ 26] Methods Trial design and participants OPTIMUM was a two-stage, participant and outcome assessor-blinded, Bayesian group sequential randomised trial, conducted at four study sites: Perth Children's Hospital (Western Australia), Murdoch Children's Research Institute (Victoria), Sydney Children's Hospital, Randwick and The Children's Hospital at Westmead (New South Wales).[ 26,27]
We enrolled healthy infants born on or after 32 weeks gestation.

They were randomised 1:1 to receive either a standard three-dose homologous pertussis priming schedule with a 6-in-1 aP combination vaccine at approximately 6 weeks, 4 months and 6 months old ('aP-only schedule') or a heterologous pertussis priming schedule consisting of a first dose of a WHO-prequalified 5-in-1 wP combination vaccine at 6 weeks old followed by the 6-in-1 aP combination vaccine at 4 months and 6 months old ('mixed wP/aP schedule').

To ensure each child received at least three primary doses of IPV while maintaining blinding, DTaP-IPV (Infanrix IPV, GlaxoSmithKline Australia; 0.5 mL intramuscular) was administered to all infants at 18 months old, in lieu of a dose of DTaP (without IPV) per the Australian NIP.

Infants with planned travel to a polio-affected region (as defined by the Global Polio Eradication Initiative) at any time before the completion of the study were ineligible at enrolment,[29] with supplementary IPV vaccination facilitated for any unplanned travel to increased risk countries before 18 months.

This trial used an adaptive group sequential design and Bayesian inference as detailed in the protocol and the statistical analysis plan.
[27] Analyses were performed according to intent-totreat with participants grouped per their randomly assigned schedule.
For all summaries and pre-specified analyses, all available outcomes were included.

The primary analysis used independent beta-binomial models to estimate the difference in probability of IgE-mediated food allergy between the two vaccine strategies; uniform priors were assumed for both response probabilities.

Secondary analyses of the primary outcome assumed a logistic regression model for occurrence of IgE-mediated food allergy, adjusting for study site, sex, breastfeeding status, birth order, parental income, mode of delivery, and family history of atopic disease at baseline.
Participants with no SPT result were assumed to not meet the primary outcome.
A sensitivity analysis excluded those with no SPT result.
A posterior probability of any reduction in IgE-mediated food allergy of at least 0.95 from the primary analysis was considered evidence of superiority of the mixed wP/aP over the aP-only schedule.
A first interim analysis was scheduled to occur after the 200th participant completed follow-up.
Additional interim analyses were to occur for every additional 200 participants unless a stopping rule was met or the maximum sample size had been reached.

At each interim analysis, the trial could be stopped for expected success or futility if the predicted probability of meeting the superiority condition was >0.95 or <0.05, respectively, based on the posterior predictive distribution from the primary analysis model.

text.text: Although the difference in results may be explained by residual bias in the earlier studies, it is important to note factors that limit transportability of the current trial results to the historical cohort examined in those studies.

First, there have been important changes in infant feeding practices; in the present trial, most parents reported the introduction of egg, cow's milk, and peanut before 12 months old in line with current recommendations.
While we had no data on feeding practice in our previous studies, Australian and international guidelines at the time recommended delayed introduction of potentially allergenic foods.

[47] Earlier introduction of allergenic foods may explain why the incidence of food allergy in the aP-only group (5.3%) was lower than anticipated (10%), albeit broadly consistent with findings from more recent Australian cohorts.

For example, the incidence of egg allergy (4.0%) fell between the estimates from other contemporaneous cohorts of Australian children (2.8% and 7.6%), [5, 43, 48] and the prevalence of peanut allergy (2.0%) was similar to that reported in another randomised trial (2.6%) and a recent observational study (2.6%). [6, 43] Secondly, variability in wP vaccine manufacturing and composition are known to influence vaccine immunogenicity and reactogenicity, [49, 50] so it is plausible that any effects on immune phenotype may also be vaccine specific.

First, OFCs were not conducted in all infants with highly probable food allergy and transient cases of IgE-mediated food allergy and eczema occurring before 12 months may have been missed, although unscheduled visits were permitted to maximise ascertainment of these events.
While it is likely there was some underascertainment of the primary outcome, there is no reason to expect any misclassification was differential between groups.
Second, blood sampling timepoints were designed to support assessment of atopic outcomes without overburdening participants.
Therefore, pre-vaccination samples were not collected to assess the contribution of baseline cytokine profiles and transplacentally derived antibodies to subsequent infant immune responses.
Finally, we were forced to terminate enrolment early due to inability to procure further doses of the wP combination vaccine.

At the last analysis the predicted probability of eventual trial success was very low (<0.01) meaning the trial would likely have stopped early for futility even if further doses could have been procured.

text.text: As a result, it is unlikely that early stopping would have affected our conclusions.

Despite these limitations, given the lack of evidence of a benefit for any endpoint or in any subgroup, we conclude that a novel mixed wP/aP schedule would be unlikely to achieve a policy-relevant reduction in the prevalence of IgE-mediated food allergy.

Our study has several strengths.
First, we conducted a closely monitored randomised comparison with blinded assessment of the primary outcome by clinical allergists, using open OFCs and other standardised diagnostic measures.
Second, the study included a geographically diverse population of Australian-born infants, with high retention rates and minimal missing data on the primary outcome.
Third, 300 infants underwent close safety monitoring and oversight, contributing robust evidence of the tolerability of 5-in-1 wP combination vaccine in infants aged 6 weeks old.
